newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns media, investors over stock rumour mill.
newsitem.headline: China warns media, investors over stock rumour mill.

text.p: China warned its financial media on Friday not to spread stock market rumours and said securities investors should be wary of inflated prices.

Measures by securities watchdogs to make China's fledgling markets less volatile had had little impact because many people spread rumours to manipulate stocks, the official Financial News said in an editorial.
"Market fluctuations have not lessened in line with the gradual standardisation of listed companies' operations," the newspaper said.
"Rather, under the assault of all kinds of rumours, fierce oscillations still regularly occur," it said, adding that stiff penalties would be given to those found spreading rumours.

Beijing has tried repeatedly to cool share speculation -- which late last year helped push one of the main indices up as much as 360 percent -- but has found it hard to cool the enthusiasm of a growing army of eager investors.

Many people claiming to be "stock experts" or "securities analysts" had tried to influence the bourses by writing articles claiming inside knowledge of stock trends or bonus share issues, the newspaper said.
"Rumours never arise for no reason, they are always linked with the interests of some small group or individual," it said.
China's financial media have carried reports all this week telling punters to be wary of fraudulent investment schemes and of speculation that could be pushing stock prices too high.
The Financial News said on Thursday that market manipulators had stirred up excitement on the nation's exchanges using false information or rumours to raise expectations.
"Some speculators...use all kinds of channels to invent all types of issues to push share prices to unimaginable highs," it said in an editorial.
Under recent amendments to the Criminal Law, charges can be brought against speculators, insider traders and those who spread market rumours, it said.
China's central bank, stung by a series of financial scandals, has warned that financial disorder threatens investors and social stability.
The People's Daily on Wednesday issued a stern warning to investors in unauthorised fund-raising schemes, saying huge fraud scandals in the early 1990s could be repeated.
The newspaper recalled a notorious 1993 case in which more than 100,000 investors put their savings into a pyramid scheme masterminded by the head of a Beijing technology firm.
The investors were lured by interest rates as high as 43 percent, but lost out badly when the scheme collapsed.
"It is regrettable that so many people in society are unbelievably forgetful," People's Daily said in an editorial.
